title: Let them be new (7:8)
hook: it's forbidden to remind someone who has returned of their past
tomorrow: if there's a world to come, do we bring our bodies?

segments.voice: Yesterday far, today close: return in a single day, and two sages arguing over who's greeted first. Today asks what everyone else does once someone has come close.

There's a story that comes out at every holiday dinner. The time your cousin set the kitchen on fire. The time someone got lost at the zoo. Everyone laughs. Usually. But once someone has truly changed, can you still tell the story of what they did? Maimonides answers, and his rule is stricter than a family dinner might guess.
screen: `THE STORY AT EVERY HOLIDAY.` → `EVERYONE LAUGHS. USUALLY.` → `FORBIDDEN TO BRING IT UP.`

segments.voice: People who return, he writes, are humble. If fools taunt them, yesterday you did this and that, they should let it go. Then he turns to everyone else, and the tone sharpens. It is utterly forbidden to say to someone who has returned: remember what you used to do. Forbidden to bring it up in front of them to shame them. Even forbidden to mention things connected to it, hints that steer them back to the memory. He files all of this under a Torah law, ona'at devarim, wronging someone with words; Leviticus says not to wrong one another. The Mishnah gives this exact example. Here's the surprise to pass on: in this law, a joke can be the violation. Not a lie, not a curse. Just a reminder. The old story may be true. It just isn't who they are now. Take smell. After a burnt dinner, a kitchen holds the smoke for days. Open the windows, cook something new, and slowly the room changes. Someone who has turned is doing that work. Every time the old story comes out, the windows close again. Let them be new.
screen: `IF FOOLS TAUNT, LET IT GO.` · `FORBIDDEN: REMEMBER WHAT YOU DID.` · `ONA'AT DEVARIM: WRONGING WITH WORDS.` · `OPEN THE WINDOWS.` · then, large: `LET THEM BE NEW.`

segments.voice: If there's water nearby, pour a little and take one slow sip, tasting it as if it were the first water you'd ever had. Then breathe in through your nose and notice what the room smells like right now, not this morning, not last week. Let the present be the only thing in your mouth and your lungs.
Let them be new: Maimonides' rule. You may not remind someone who has returned of who they used to be.
Something to keep: let them be new; the old story may be true, but it isn't theirs anymore. Twenty-one down, nine to go.

howItsDone: Jewish law counts hurtful words as ona'at devarim, a real wrong; Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 names reminding a returner of their past as an example, and it's taught in study of the laws of speech.
